samples.text:
The line graph illustrates the proportion of households in Arden, Belmont and Calder that used public bicycles at least once a week from 2010 to 2025.

Overall, the use of public bicycles increased in Arden and Calder, while it decreased in Belmont after 2015. By 2025, Arden had the highest percentage.

In 2010, Belmont had the largest figure at 20%, compared with 12% in Arden and only 5% in Calder. Over the next five years, all three cities saw a rise, and Belmont reached a peak of 26% in 2015.

After that, the trends were different. The percentage in Arden continued to grow steadily, reaching 27% in 2020 and 35% in 2025. Calder also increased quickly, from 11% to 22% in 2020, the same level as Belmont, and then to 30% at the end of the period. In contrast, Belmont fell to 22% in 2020 and dropped further to 18% in 2025, which was the lowest of the three cities.

samples.text:
The line graph compares the percentage of households in three cities, Arden, Belmont and Calder, that used public bicycles at least weekly between 2010 and 2025.

Overall, public bicycle use grew substantially in Arden and Calder, whereas Belmont, which started as the leading city, saw its figure decline after 2015. As a result, Belmont went from first to last place over the period.

At the beginning of the period, one in five households in Belmont (20%) used the bicycles weekly, well ahead of Arden (12%) and Calder (5%). Belmont's figure continued to rise to a peak of 26% in 2015, but then fell back steadily, finishing at 18% in 2025.

Arden, by contrast, recorded consistent growth throughout, almost tripling from 12% to 35% and overtaking Belmont shortly after 2015. The most dramatic change, however, occurred in Calder, where usage climbed from just 5% to 30%, a sixfold increase. Calder drew level with Belmont at 22% in 2020 before moving clearly ahead of it by the end of the period.

samples.text:
The graph tracks the share of households in Arden, Belmont and Calder that used public bicycles at least once a week over a fifteen-year period from 2010.

The most notable feature is a reversal in the cities' positions: Belmont, initially the leader, ended the period with the lowest rate, while Arden and Calder both saw sustained growth. Arden had the highest figure by 2025.

In 2010, weekly use stood at 20% of households in Belmont, against 12% in Arden and a mere 5% in Calder. Belmont's lead widened slightly to 2015, when its rate peaked at 26%, but the figure then declined in each subsequent five-year interval, to 22% and finally 18%.

The other two cities moved in the opposite direction. Arden's rate rose steadily at every point, almost tripling to 35% and passing Belmont at some point between 2015 and 2020. Calder's growth was even more pronounced in relative terms: from a very low base, its figure doubled to 11% by 2015 and doubled again to 22% in 2020, matching Belmont, before reaching 30%, six times its starting level.

samples.text:
The graph shows how the proportion of households using public bicycles at least weekly changed in three cities, Arden, Belmont and Calder, between 2010 and 2025.

The period was marked by a striking reversal: Belmont, the clear leader in 2010, finished with the lowest rate of the three, while Arden and Calder grew so strongly that Arden ended the period well ahead.

Belmont began with weekly use among 20% of households and extended its lead to 26% by 2015. From that peak, however, its figure fell at each subsequent measurement, to 22% in 2020 and 18% in 2025, slightly below where it had started.

Arden, starting at 12%, grew without interruption, rising to 18%, then 27% and finally 35%, almost three times its initial level. Calder's rise was steeper still in relative terms. From only 5% in 2010, its rate roughly doubled in each of the first two intervals, reaching 22% in 2020, the point at which it drew level with Belmont, and then climbed to 30%, six times the original figure, leaving Belmont twelve percentage points behind.
